title: Tokenizing Pieces: The Loop Algorithm
description: Very hard trace-through questions on the digit-grouping loop algorithm: how 'current' and 'pieces' behave step by step, edge cases at the start/end of a string, and the '0'-'9' Unicode comparison quirk.

questions.question: Tracing the algorithm exactly as written, what is the final `pieces` array produced for the input string "3*(9 + 5) + 45" once spaces have been filtered out (splitted = ['3','*','(','9','+','5',')','+','4','5'])?
questions.explanation: Only the trailing '4','5' are adjacent digits with nothing separating them, so they merge into '45' via the leftover `current` push. '9' and '5' each sit next to non-digits ('+' and ')') so they stay as single-digit pieces, and ')' is never merged into a digit's piece.

questions.question: Using the same algorithm, what would `pieces` be for the input "12+345"?
questions.explanation: Consecutive digits before the '+' accumulate into '12', get flushed when '+' is hit, and the trailing digits '3','4','5' accumulate into '345', flushed by the final `if (current)` check after the loop ends.

questions.question: In the string "5+*3", two non-digit characters ('+' and '*') sit back-to-back. What does the algorithm produce as the final `pieces` array?
questions.explanation: Only digit characters ever accumulate inside `current`. Every non-digit character is pushed to `pieces` on its own the moment it's encountered, so '+' and '*' can never merge with each other even though they're adjacent.

questions.question: For the input "5+" (a digit immediately followed by a non-digit, with nothing after it), what is the final `pieces` array once the loop AND the trailing `if (current)` check both finish running?
questions.explanation: When '+' is reached, current ('5') is flushed into pieces and then '+' itself is pushed. current is now empty, so the trailing `if (current)` check after the loop has nothing left to add.

questions.question: Why does the algorithm need the `if (current) { pieces.push(current) }` line placed after the for-loop finishes?
options: To push any leftover run of digits still sitting in `current` that never got flushed inside the loop, which happens whenever the string ends on a digit
To make sure any leading whitespace at the start of the string gets removed before pieces are counted
To reverse the order of the `pieces` array so digits always come first
To immediately push every non-digit character that appears at the very end of the string
questions.explanation: Inside the loop, `current` is only flushed when a non-digit character is encountered. If the string ends while `current` still holds digits (no trailing non-digit to trigger the flush), that final check is the only thing that pushes it into `pieces`.

questions.question: Per the callout, why does `splitted[i] >= '0' && splitted[i] <= '9'` correctly detect digit characters in JavaScript?
options: Because JavaScript automatically parses any string that looks like a digit into an actual Number type before comparison
Because '0' and '9' are reserved keywords that only match numeric characters

Because during the >= and <= comparisons, JavaScript converts the string characters to their underlying Unicode number values, effectively checking whether the character falls within that numeric range
Because the >= and <= operators only work on arrays, not individual characters, forcing an implicit type conversion
questions.explanation: The callout explicitly states that during >= and <= comparisons, JavaScript converts the strings to their Unicode number equivalents, which is what makes the range check work.

questions.question: According to the callout, why would the exact same `n >= '0' && n <= '9'` check fail to work as intended if translated directly into other programming languages?
options: Because other languages don't allow the `&&` operator to be used with comparisons
Because most other languages don't support the greater-than-or-equal-to operator at all
Because '0' and '9' would be interpreted as separate arrays in most other languages
Because in those other languages, '0' and '9' remain plain strings rather than being converted to numbers during the comparison, so the range check wouldn't behave the same way
questions.explanation: The callout notes this specific comparison trick relies on JavaScript's behavior of treating '0' and '9' as numbers during the comparison — a conversion that doesn't happen the same way in other languages.

questions.question: Before the algorithm ever begins looping through the characters, what do steps 1 and 2 say to set up first?
options: Convert the entire input string to uppercase and remove all symbols
Create an empty list called pieces, and an empty string called current
Split the string into individual digits only, discarding every non-digit character
Create a counter variable starting at 1 and a boolean flag set to false
questions.explanation: Steps 1 and 2 of the algorithm are to create an empty `pieces` list and an empty `current` string, before any character is examined.

questions.question: Based on the intuition section, which pair of adjacent characters would actually get merged into the same 'piece' by this algorithm?
options: Two adjacent symbol characters, like '+' followed by '*'
A digit character immediately followed by a symbol character, like '9' followed by '+'
Two adjacent digit characters, like '4' followed by '5'
A symbol character immediately followed by a digit character, like '(' followed by '9'
questions.explanation: The core intuition is that a number followed by another number forms a single piece. Any pairing involving a symbol never merges, since symbols are always pushed as their own piece.

questions.question: For the (space-filtered) input "9(8", what is the final `pieces` array the algorithm produces?
questions.explanation: '9' is flushed and '(' is pushed the moment the non-digit is hit, then '8' accumulates in current and gets flushed by the trailing `if (current)` check. The symbol never merges with either digit.
